decks.title: Depreciation — Part 1: Meaning, Causes and the Two Methods
goals: Explain what depreciation is, why it is charged and what causes it
Calculate yearly depreciation by the straight line and written down value methods, including part years counted in months
Compare the two methods and say which suits which kind of asset

slides.heading: Depreciation: spreading the cost of an asset
slides.body_md: Part 1: why a fixed asset loses value, what causes it, and how the **straight line** and **written down value** methods work.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why fixed assets lose value, the causes and objectives of depreciation, the three factors that decide the amount, the straight line method, the written down value method and a comparison of the two methods
visual.caption: Where Part 1 goes

slides.narration: Welcome. A machine or a van does not last for ever. Each year the business uses up a part of it. In this part we see why that loss must be charged as an expense, what causes it, and the two main ways of working it out.

slides.heading: What depreciation means
bullets: Depreciation is the **fall in the book value** of a fixed asset because it is used up.
It spreads the **cost** of the asset over its useful life.
It is a **non-cash** charge made every year.

rows: The value of a fixed asset in the books goes down because the asset is used up
The cost of the asset is spread over the years in which it helps to earn income
No money leaves the business when depreciation is charged; it is an expense of the year
The charge is made whether the firm earns a profit or a loss

visual.alt: Table of four features of depreciation: a fall in the book value of a fixed asset, an allocation of its cost over its useful life, a non-cash charge, and a charge made every year

slides.narration: Depreciation is the fall in the book value of a fixed asset caused by its use. It spreads the cost of the asset over the years the asset serves. No cash leaves the business when depreciation is charged, and the charge is made every year, even in a year of loss.

slides.heading: Why depreciation must be charged
slides.body_md: Without depreciation the **profit is overstated** and the asset is shown at too high a value.

rows: The cost of using the asset is an expense of the year; without it profit is overstated
The balance sheet shows the asset at cost less the amount used up so far
Lower profit means lower drawings, so money stays to replace the asset later
The expense falls in the same years as the income that the asset helps to earn

visual.alt: Table of four reasons depreciation must be charged: to find the correct profit, to show the asset at its true value, to keep funds in the business for replacement, and to match the expense with the income of the year
visual.caption: Why depreciation must be charged

slides.narration: There are four reasons to charge depreciation. It gives the correct profit, because using an asset has a cost. It shows the asset at its true value in the balance sheet. It keeps funds in the business, since lower profit means lower drawings. And it matches expense with income.

slides.heading: Causes of depreciation
bullets: **Wear and tear** from use and exposure
**Passage of time** for assets with a fixed term
**Obsolescence** when something better arrives
**Depletion** of a wasting asset such as a quarry

rows: Physical use and exposure wear the asset out
A delivery van of Kanpur Couriers is driven every day for three years
An asset with a fixed term loses value as the term runs out
A lease of a workshop held by Anantnag Metals shortens every year
New inventions or fashions make the asset out of date before it is worn out
Machines of Silvassa Prints are replaced by faster models
A wasting asset is used up as the resource is taken out
A stone quarry of Jaisalmer Granites yields less each year

visual.alt: Table of four causes of depreciation with an example of each: wear and tear, passage of time, obsolescence and depletion
visual.caption: The four causes of depreciation

slides.narration: Four causes. Wear and tear comes from daily use. Passage of time reduces the value of an asset with a fixed term, such as a lease. Obsolescence makes a machine out of date even if it still works. Depletion uses up a wasting asset like a quarry.

slides.heading: Characteristics of depreciation
slides.body_md: Depreciation applies to **fixed assets with a limited life**. It is not repairs, and it is not the same as a fall in market price.

rows: Applies to fixed assets with a limited life
Plant, furniture, vehicles, buildings and the like
Land does not wear out, so no depreciation is normally charged on it
Repairs keep the asset in working order; depreciation spreads its cost
Different from a fall in market price
Depreciation follows the cost and the plan, not the daily market value
Life and residual value are estimated when the asset is bought

visual.alt: Table of five characteristics of depreciation: it applies to fixed assets with a limited life, it is not charged on land, it differs from repairs, it differs from a fall in market price, and it rests on estimates

slides.narration: Remember what depreciation is not. It is not charged on land. It is not the cost of repairs. It does not follow the daily market price. It rests on estimates of life and residual value made when the asset is bought.

slides.heading: Quick check: a cause of depreciation
slides.body_md: Choose the cause.
slides.narration: A machine still works perfectly, but a faster model has come into the market and the owner plans to replace it soon. Think about which cause of depreciation this describes, and then choose.

slides.heading: Three factors decide the amount
slides.body_md: The yearly charge depends on the **cost**, the **estimated life** and the **residual value**.

rows: Purchase price plus carriage, installation and other cost of making it ready for use
A higher cost gives a higher charge
The number of years the firm expects to use the asset
A longer life gives a lower charge
What the asset is expected to fetch when it is finally sold
A higher scrap value gives a lower charge

visual.alt: Table of the three factors that decide the amount of depreciation: cost, estimated useful life and residual or scrap value, each with its effect on the yearly charge
visual.caption: Three factors decide the amount

slides.narration: The yearly charge depends on three factors. The cost includes everything spent to bring the asset into use. The estimated useful life is the number of years of service. The residual value is the scrap price at the end. A higher cost raises the charge, a longer life or higher scrap value lowers it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: straight line from cost, scrap and life
slides.body_md: **Tindivanam Tiles**, an imagined firm, buys a kiln for ₹8,00,000. It expects to use it for 6 years and then sell it as scrap for ₹80,000. Find the yearly depreciation and the rate.

visual.alt: Straight line depreciation of a kiln of Tindivanam Tiles, an imagined firm: one lakh twenty thousand rupees every year for six years, taking the book value from eight lakh rupees down to the scrap value of eighty thousand rupees
visual.caption: Tindivanam Tiles: the same charge every year

slides.narration: The kiln costs rupees eight lakh and will fetch rupees eighty thousand as scrap. The amount to be written off is the difference, rupees seven lakh twenty thousand. Spread over six years, that is rupees one lakh twenty thousand every year. This is fifteen per cent of the cost. After six years the book value equals the scrap value.

slides.heading: The straight line method
slides.body_md: The same amount is charged **every year**, on the **original cost**.

rows: Annual charge ÷ cost × 100, a fixed percentage of the original cost
Falls by an equal amount each year and reaches the scrap value at the end of the life

visual.alt: Table of four points on the straight line method: equal yearly charge, the formula using cost, scrap value and life, a rate on original cost, and a book value that falls evenly to the scrap value
visual.caption: The straight line method

slides.narration: In the straight line method the charge is the same every year. The formula is cost less scrap value, divided by the life in years. The rate is a fixed percentage of the original cost. The book value falls evenly and reaches the scrap value at the end of the life.

slides.heading: The written down value method
slides.body_md: A fixed **percentage of the opening book value** is charged each year, so the charge **falls** as the asset ages.

rows: A fixed percentage of the book value at the start of each year
Opening book value × rate; it is highest in the first year and falls every year
Never reaches zero by itself; it is multiplied by (1 − rate) every year
Not used in the calculation of the yearly charge

visual.alt: Table of four points on the written down value method: a fixed percentage on the opening book value, a charge that falls every year, a book value that never reaches zero, and no use of scrap value in the calculation
visual.caption: The written down value method

slides.narration: In the written down value method a fixed percentage is applied to the book value at the start of each year. The charge is highest in the first year and falls every year. The book value is multiplied by one minus the rate each year, so it never reaches zero by itself. Scrap value is not used in the calculation.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: written down value for four years
slides.body_md: **Pollachi Feeds**, an imagined firm, buys a machine for ₹6,40,000 and writes it down at 25% a year on the written down value. Find the charge for each of four years.

visual.alt: Written down value depreciation at twenty five per cent on a machine of Pollachi Feeds, an imagined firm, costing six lakh forty thousand rupees: charges of one lakh sixty thousand, one lakh twenty thousand, ninety thousand and sixty seven thousand five hundred rupees in four years, leaving two lakh two thousand five hundred rupees
visual.caption: Pollachi Feeds: the charge falls every year

slides.narration: Each year the rate is applied to what is left. Year one, twenty five per cent of rupees six lakh forty thousand is rupees one lakh sixty thousand. The book value falls to rupees four lakh eighty thousand. Year two, the charge is rupees one lakh twenty thousand. Year three, rupees ninety thousand. Year four, rupees sixty seven thousand five hundred. After four years rupees two lakh two thousand five hundred remain.

slides.heading: Quick check: written down value
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Read the statement about the written down value method. Think about what the rate is applied to in each year, and whether the charge stays the same.

slides.heading: Part-year depreciation: count the months
slides.body_md: When an asset is bought or sold during the year, charge depreciation only for the **months it was in use**: **annual charge × months ÷ 12**.

nodes.label: Note the date of purchase or sale
Count whole months in the year
Add the part-year charge to the asset

visual.alt: Route map for part-year depreciation: note the date of purchase or sale, count the whole months in the year, multiply the annual charge by the months and divide by twelve, and record the part-year charge
visual.caption: Part-year depreciation in four steps

slides.narration: If an asset is bought part-way through the year, it is used for only some months. Count the whole months from the date of purchase to the end of the year. Multiply the annual charge by that number of months and divide by twelve. The same rule applies up to the date of a sale.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: bought part-way through the year
slides.body_md: **Bhimavaram Fisheries**, an imagined firm, buys a cold room for ₹3,60,000 on **1 August 2026**. Books close on 31 March and depreciation is 10% a year. Find the charge for the first two years by both methods.
bullets: Months from 1 August 2026 to 31 March 2027 = **8**.
First year, both methods: 3,60,000 × 10% × 8/12 = ₹24,000.
Second year: straight line 36,000; written down value 33,600 (10% of 3,36,000).

visual.alt: Depreciation on a cold room of Bhimavaram Fisheries, an imagined firm, bought on 1 August 2026 for three lakh sixty thousand rupees: twenty four thousand rupees in the first year of eight months under both methods, and then thirty six thousand rupees by the straight line method against thirty three thousand six hundred rupees by the written down value method
visual.caption: Bhimavaram Fisheries: a purchase part-way through the year

slides.narration: August to March is eight months. In the first year both methods give the same charge, rupees twenty four thousand, because the base is the cost. In the second year the straight line method again charges rupees thirty six thousand, but the written down value method charges ten per cent of rupees three lakh thirty six thousand, which is rupees thirty three thousand six hundred.

slides.heading: Same rate, two methods
slides.body_md: At the same rate the first year is the same. Later the **straight line** charge stays level and the **written down value** charge falls.

visual.alt: Comparison of the two methods on a press of Hubballi Hydraulics, an imagined firm, costing six lakh twenty five thousand rupees at twenty per cent for five years: the straight line charge stays at one lakh twenty five thousand rupees while the written down value charge falls from one lakh twenty five thousand to fifty one thousand two hundred rupees, leaving a book value of two lakh four thousand eight hundred rupees
visual.caption: Hubballi Hydraulics: the same rate, two methods

slides.narration: Here is one press at twenty per cent for five years. The straight line charge stays at one lakh twenty five thousand rupees. The written down value charge starts at the same amount and falls to fifty one thousand two hundred rupees. After five years the straight line method has written the press off completely, while a book value remains under the written down value method.

slides.heading: Quick check: completing the rule
slides.body_md: Complete the sentence.
slides.narration: Look at the formula for the straight line method. Think about what is taken away from the cost before dividing by the life, and then fill in the blanks.

slides.heading: Advantages and limitations of each method
slides.body_md: No method is best for every asset; each has **advantages** and **limitations**.

rows: Simple to calculate; equal charge every year; asset can be written down to its scrap value
Heavier charge when the asset is new and repairs are low; total of depreciation and repairs stays level; accepted for tax
Ignores the rise in repairs as the asset ages, so the total charge grows; charges the same amount although the asset gives less service as it ages; ignores interest on the money invested in the asset
Book value never becomes zero; the charge in the early years is heavy; calculation is longer

visual.alt: Table of advantages and limitations of the straight line method and the written down value method
visual.caption: Advantages and limitations

slides.narration: The straight line method is simple and gives an equal charge every year, but it ignores the fact that repairs rise as an asset ages. The written down value method charges more when the asset is new and repairs are low, so the total burden stays level. Its book value never becomes zero, and the calculation is longer.

slides.heading: Choosing a method
slides.body_md: Choose the method by **how the asset gives its service**.

rows: They give about the same service each year of a fixed life
Use is even and repairs stay small
They lose value fastest early and need more repairs later
Most of the cost is recovered in the early years

visual.alt: Table matching four kinds of asset with the method that suits them: leases, patents and buildings and furniture suit straight line; vehicles, computers and machinery and quickly obsolete assets suit written down value
visual.caption: Which method suits which asset

slides.narration: Assets that give even service over a fixed life, such as leases, patents, buildings and furniture, suit the straight line method. Vehicles, computers and machinery lose value fastest early and need more repairs later, so the written down value method suits them. A quickly outdated asset also suits it.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: A fall in book value; a non-cash allocation of cost over the useful life
Wear and tear, passage of time, obsolescence, depletion
(Cost − scrap) ÷ life: the same amount every year, on original cost
Rate × opening book value: a falling charge
Annual charge × months ÷ 12, counting the months exactly

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning, causes, factors, the straight line method, the written down value method and part-year depreciation

slides.narration: To sum up. Depreciation is a fall in the book value of a fixed asset, spread over its life. Its causes are wear and tear, passage of time, obsolescence and depletion. The amount depends on cost, life and residual value. The straight line method charges the same amount every year. The written down value method charges a percentage of the falling book value.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Show the **formula** before the figures: (cost − scrap) ÷ life for straight line; rate × opening book value for written down value.
Count the **months exactly**; write the months in the working, for example 8/12.
For the written down value method, apply the rate to the **book value of that year**, never to the cost after year one.
Name each **cause of depreciation** and add a one-line example when the question asks for causes.
slides.narration: In the examination, write the formula first and then the figures. Show the months used in a part year. Under the written down value method always apply the rate to the book value at the start of the year. When asked for causes, name each one and give a short example.

decks.title: Depreciation — Part 2: Recording, Additions and Sale of Assets
goals: Record depreciation in the asset account and through a provision for depreciation account, over two or three years
Charge depreciation on an asset added during the year
Find the profit or loss on sale, with and without an asset disposal account

slides.heading: Recording depreciation and selling assets
slides.body_md: Part 2: **charging depreciation to the asset** or to a **provision account**, **additions** during the year, and the **sale** of an asset.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the two ways of recording depreciation, charging it to the asset account, using a provision for depreciation account, additions during the year, sale of an asset and the asset disposal account
visual.caption: Where Part 2 goes

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Now we put depreciation into the books. There are two ways of recording it. After that we look at assets added during the year and at the sale of an asset, with the profit or loss on sale, with and without an asset disposal account.

slides.heading: Two ways of recording depreciation
slides.body_md: Depreciation can be **credited to the asset account**, or to a **provision for depreciation account** while the asset stays at cost.

rows: Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset A/c
Depreciation A/c Dr; To Provision for Depreciation A/c
Original cost, until the asset is sold
Shown in the provision account, growing every year
Asset at cost, less the provision, giving book value
Depreciation for the year is debited
Depreciation for the year is debited

visual.alt: Table comparing the two ways of recording depreciation: the journal entry, what the asset account shows, whether accumulated depreciation appears, the balance sheet and the profit and loss account
visual.caption: Two ways of recording depreciation

slides.narration: In the first way, depreciation is credited to the asset account itself, so the asset shows its book value. In the second way, the asset stays at cost and depreciation is credited to a provision for depreciation account. In both ways, the profit and loss account is debited with the depreciation of the year.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: depreciation charged to the asset
slides.body_md: **Sivaganga Stationers**, an imagined firm, buys furniture for ₹2,60,000 on 1 April 2026 and depreciates it at 15% a year on cost, crediting the asset. Pass the entries for the first year.
bullets: The charge is moved to the profit and loss account at the year end.

rows: *(Being depreciation for the year charged to the asset)*
*(Being depreciation transferred to Profit and Loss A/c)*

visual.alt: Journal entries of Sivaganga Stationers, an imagined firm, for the year ended 31 March 2027: the purchase of furniture for two lakh sixty thousand rupees, depreciation of thirty nine thousand rupees charged to the asset, and its transfer to the profit and loss account
visual.caption: Sivaganga Stationers: journal entries for the first year

slides.narration: The furniture is bought for rupees two lakh sixty thousand. Fifteen per cent of the cost is rupees thirty nine thousand. The entry debits depreciation and credits furniture. At the year end depreciation is closed by debiting the profit and loss account. The furniture now stands at rupees two lakh twenty one thousand.

slides.heading: Worked example 1 continued: the asset account over three years
slides.body_md: The same charge is made every year, so the balance falls by the same amount.

visual.alt: Furniture account of Sivaganga Stationers for three years, with depreciation of thirty nine thousand rupees credited each year, so that the balance carried down falls from two lakh twenty one thousand to one lakh eighty two thousand and then to one lakh forty three thousand rupees
visual.caption: Sivaganga Stationers: the Furniture account for three years

slides.narration: Each year the account opens with the balance brought down, and depreciation of rupees thirty nine thousand is credited. The balance carried down is rupees two lakh twenty one thousand after the first year, rupees one lakh eighty two thousand after the second and rupees one lakh forty three thousand after the third. That last amount is the book value shown in the balance sheet.

slides.heading: The provision method step by step
slides.body_md: The **asset account never shows depreciation**. The **provision account** collects it year after year.

rows: Asset A/c Dr; To Bank A/c
Asset is recorded at cost and stays at cost
Depreciation A/c Dr; To Provision for Depreciation A/c
The provision grows by the year's charge
Profit and Loss A/c Dr; To Depreciation A/c
The balance is the book value

visual.alt: Table of the steps of the provision method: buy the asset at cost, charge depreciation to the provision account, close depreciation to the profit and loss account, and show the asset at cost less the provision in the balance sheet
visual.caption: The provision method in four steps

slides.narration: In the provision method the asset account is not touched by depreciation. Each year depreciation is debited and the provision for depreciation account is credited. At the end of the year depreciation is closed to the profit and loss account. In the balance sheet the asset is shown at cost, with the provision deducted.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: machinery at cost and the provision
slides.body_md: **Nanded Nurseries**, an imagined firm, buys machinery for ₹4,80,000 on 1 April 2026 and depreciates it at 15% a year on the written down value, keeping a provision account. Show the accounts for three years.
bullets: Machinery A/c stays at 4,80,000 each year.

visual.alt: Machinery account of Nanded Nurseries, an imagined firm, for three years: it stays at the cost of four lakh eighty thousand rupees every year because depreciation is not credited to it
visual.caption: Nanded Nurseries: the Machinery account stays at cost

slides.narration: Machinery was bought for rupees four lakh eighty thousand and stays in the asset account at that cost in every year. Depreciation is not credited to it. So the account looks the same at the end of each year. The depreciation goes to the provision account instead.

slides.heading: Worked example 2 continued: the provision account
slides.body_md: After three years the provision stands at **₹1,85,220**, and the book value is ₹4,80,000 − ₹1,85,220 = **₹2,94,780**.

rows: **Provision for Depreciation A/c, year ended 31 March 2027**
**Provision for Depreciation A/c, year ended 31 March 2028**
**Provision for Depreciation A/c, year ended 31 March 2029**

visual.alt: Provision for Depreciation account of Nanded Nurseries for three years: depreciation of seventy two thousand, sixty one thousand two hundred and fifty two thousand twenty rupees is credited, and the balance grows to one lakh eighty five thousand two hundred twenty rupees
visual.caption: Nanded Nurseries: the provision grows every year

slides.narration: Written down value depreciation is fifteen per cent of rupees four lakh eighty thousand, which is rupees seventy two thousand, in the first year. In the second year it is fifteen per cent of rupees four lakh eight thousand, which is rupees sixty one thousand two hundred. In the third year it is rupees fifty two thousand twenty. The provision grows to rupees one lakh eighty five thousand two hundred twenty. Cost less provision leaves a book value of rupees two lakh ninety four thousand seven hundred eighty.

slides.heading: Quick check: the provision account
slides.body_md: Choose the correct answer.
slides.narration: A firm keeps its machinery at cost and credits depreciation to a provision account. Think about what the balance sheet shows for the machinery at the end of the year, and then choose.

slides.heading: Additions during the year
slides.body_md: Charge the **old assets** for the full year and the **new asset** only for the months it was in use.

nodes.label: Old assets get the full year

visual.alt: Route map for an addition during the year: note the date of purchase, count the months to 31 March, work out the part-year charge, and give the old assets the full-year charge
visual.caption: Depreciation when an asset is added

slides.narration: When an asset is added during the year, the old assets are depreciated for the full year. The new asset is depreciated only from the date of purchase. Count the months to the end of the year, multiply the annual charge by that number and divide by twelve.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: plant added in the second year
slides.body_md: **Vizianagaram Vessels**, an imagined firm, has plant costing ₹3,20,000 bought on 1 April 2026. It buys new plant for ₹1,60,000 on **1 October 2027**. Depreciation is 10% a year on cost, credited to the plant account. Find the charge for each year.

visual.alt: Depreciation of Vizianagaram Vessels, an imagined firm, on its old plant of three lakh twenty thousand rupees and a new plant of one lakh sixty thousand rupees bought on 1 October 2027: thirty two thousand rupees in the first year, forty thousand in the second including eight thousand for six months on the new plant, and forty eight thousand in the third
visual.caption: Vizianagaram Vessels: depreciation by plant and year

slides.narration: The old plant is charged for the full year every year, rupees thirty two thousand. The new plant was bought on the first of October, so it was used for six months in the second year. Ten per cent of rupees one lakh sixty thousand for six months is rupees eight thousand. The second year total is therefore rupees forty thousand, and the third year total is rupees forty eight thousand.

slides.heading: Worked example 3 continued: the plant account, second year
slides.body_md: Opening balance, the new purchase and the full year's charge appear in **one account**.

visual.alt: Plant account of Vizianagaram Vessels for the year ended 31 March 2028: opening balance two lakh eighty eight thousand rupees, purchase of one lakh sixty thousand rupees, depreciation of forty thousand rupees, and a balance carried down of four lakh eight thousand rupees
visual.caption: Plant account, year ended 31 March 2028

slides.narration: The plant account opens with rupees two lakh eighty eight thousand, the book value of the old plant. The new plant adds rupees one lakh sixty thousand. The year's depreciation of rupees forty thousand is credited. The balance carried down is rupees four lakh eight thousand, and it becomes the opening balance of the third year.

slides.heading: Sale of an asset: book value, profit and loss
bullets: Charge depreciation **up to the date of sale**.
**Book value** = cost − accumulated depreciation.
Sale price > book value: **profit**; sale price < book value: **loss**.

rows: Book value on the date of sale
Cost − accumulated depreciation up to that date
Sale price greater than the book value
Sale price smaller than the book value
Profit and loss account: a profit is credited and a loss is debited

visual.alt: Table of how book value, profit and loss on sale are found and where the result is recorded
visual.caption: Profit or loss on sale

slides.narration: When an asset is sold, first charge depreciation up to the date of sale, counting the months used in that year. The book value is cost less all depreciation to that date. If the sale price is more than the book value there is a profit, and if it is less there is a loss. The result is taken to the profit and loss account.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a loss on sale, no disposal account
slides.body_md: **Aizawl Appliances**, an imagined firm, bought machine A for ₹3,00,000 on 1 April 2026 and machine B for ₹1,60,000 on 1 October 2026. It writes machinery down at 20% on the written down value, crediting the asset. Machine B is sold on **1 July 2028** for ₹1,00,000. Find the loss on sale.
bullets: Book value of B on 1 July 2028 = **₹1,09,440**.

visual.alt: Working for machine B of Aizawl Appliances, an imagined firm, bought for one lakh sixty thousand rupees on 1 October 2026 at twenty per cent on the written down value: sixteen thousand, twenty eight thousand eight hundred and five thousand seven hundred sixty rupees, leaving one lakh nine thousand four hundred forty rupees on 1 July 2028
visual.caption: Aizawl Appliances: machine B up to the date of sale

slides.narration: Machine B was used for six months in the first year, twelve in the second, and three in the third, up to the first of July. The charges are rupees sixteen thousand, rupees twenty eight thousand eight hundred and rupees five thousand seven hundred sixty. The book value on the day of sale is rupees one lakh nine thousand four hundred forty. It was sold for rupees one lakh, so the loss is rupees nine thousand four hundred forty.

slides.heading: Worked example 4 continued: the Machinery account
slides.body_md: Machine A has 38,400 of depreciation for the year, and machine B 5,760, so the account is credited with ₹44,160.

rows: By Bank A/c (sale of machine B, 1 July 2028)
By Profit and Loss A/c (loss on sale)

visual.alt: Machinery account of Aizawl Appliances for the year ended 31 March 2029, with depreciation of forty four thousand one hundred sixty rupees, sale proceeds of one lakh rupees, a loss on sale of nine thousand four hundred forty rupees and a balance carried down of one lakh fifty three thousand six hundred rupees
visual.caption: Aizawl Appliances: the Machinery account in the year of sale

slides.narration: In the year of sale the machinery account opens with the book value of both machines. Depreciation of rupees forty four thousand one hundred sixty is credited, being the charge on machine A for the year and on machine B up to the date of sale. The sale proceeds are credited too, and the loss on sale is credited as well. The balance carried down is the book value of machine A, rupees one lakh fifty three thousand six hundred.

slides.heading: Quick check: profit or loss
slides.body_md: True or false?

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and need for depreciation
sections.body_md:
A fixed asset such as a machine, a van or furniture serves the business for several years and is used up as it serves. **Depreciation** is the fall in the **book value** of the asset caused by that use, and the amount for each year is charged as an expense.

- It spreads the **cost** of the asset over its useful life.
- It is a **non-cash** charge: nothing is paid when it is recorded.
- It is charged **every year**, whether the firm earns a profit or a loss.

**Why charge it?** To find the **correct profit** (the cost of using the asset is an expense), to show the asset at its **true value**, to keep **funds in the business** (lower profit means lower drawings) and to **match** the expense with the income it helps to earn.

key_terms.definition_md: The fall in the book value of a fixed asset because it is used, charged as an expense of each year.
Cost of the asset less the depreciation charged on it so far.
An asset bought to be used in the business for more than one year, not to be resold in the ordinary course.

sections.heading: 2. Causes and characteristics
sections.body_md:
Four causes make an asset lose value:

1. **Wear and tear:** physical use and exposure.
2. **Passage of time:** an asset with a fixed term, such as a lease, shortens every year.
3. **Obsolescence:** a better design makes the asset out of date even if it still works.
4. **Depletion:** a wasting asset such as a quarry or mine is used up as the resource is taken out.

**Characteristics:** depreciation applies to fixed assets with a limited life; land is normally not depreciated; it is different from **repairs** (which keep the asset working) and from a **fall in market price**; it rests on **estimates** of life and scrap value.

sections.heading: 3. Factors and the straight line method
sections.body_md:
The amount depends on three factors:

- **Cost** (price plus carriage, installation and other cost of bringing the asset into use);
- **estimated useful life** in years;
- **residual (scrap) value** at the end of the life.

**Straight line method:** the same amount every year.

**Annual depreciation = (Cost − Scrap value) ÷ Life in years**

**Rate on cost = Annual depreciation ÷ Cost × 100**

The book value falls evenly and reaches the scrap value at the end of the life.

key_terms.definition_md: The amount the asset is expected to fetch when it is finally sold or scrapped; also called scrap or salvage value.
A method that charges the same amount every year, found from cost, scrap value and life.

rows: Annual charge ÷ cost × 100, a fixed percentage of the original cost
Falls by an equal amount each year and reaches the scrap value at the end of the life

sections.heading: 4. Written down value method and part-year depreciation
sections.body_md:
**Written down value (WDV) method:** a fixed percentage of the **opening book value** of each year.

**Depreciation of the year = Rate × Opening book value**

The charge is highest in the first year and **falls** every year; the book value is multiplied by (1 − rate) each year and never reaches nil. Scrap value is not used in the yearly charge.

**Part years.** When an asset is bought or sold during the year, count the whole **months of use** and charge **annual depreciation × months ÷ 12**. An asset bought on 1 August 2026 and a year ending 31 March 2027 has 8 months. Under WDV, the second year is a full year on the book value left after the part-year charge.

Depreciation for only the months in a year in which the asset was used.

sections.heading: 5. Comparing the two methods
sections.body_md:
At the same rate, the **first full year** gives the same charge, because both apply the rate to the cost. After that the **straight line** charge stays level while the **WDV** charge falls. The straight line method writes the asset down to its scrap value; the WDV method always leaves a balance.

**Straight line:** simple, an equal charge each year; but it ignores the rise in repairs as the asset ages.

**WDV:** a heavy charge early (when repairs are low) and a light one later (when repairs are high), so the total burden stays more even; but the book value never becomes nil and the working is longer.

**Choice:** straight line suits leases, patents, buildings and furniture; WDV suits vehicles, computers and machinery, and assets that become out of date quickly.

sections.heading: 6. Recording depreciation: asset account and provision account
sections.body_md:
**Method 1 — credited to the asset account.**

Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset A/c. The asset account shows the **book value**, falling every year. At the year end: Profit and Loss A/c Dr; To Depreciation A/c.

**Method 2 — provision for depreciation account (accumulated depreciation).**

Depreciation A/c Dr; To Provision for Depreciation A/c. The asset account stays at **cost**; the provision grows each year. In the balance sheet: **asset at cost less provision = book value**.

In both methods the Profit and Loss A/c is debited with the year's depreciation, and the book value is the same. Every account is balanced with **balance c/d** and brought down as **balance b/d**.

sections.heading: 7. Additions and sale of assets
sections.body_md:
**Additions.** Depreciate the old assets for the full year; depreciate the new asset only for the **months from the date of purchase**.

**Sale.** Follow four steps: (1) charge depreciation **up to the date of sale**, counting months; (2) find the **book value** = cost − accumulated depreciation; (3) compare it with the **sale price**; (4) a price above book value is a **profit**, below it is a **loss**.

**Profit or loss on sale = Sale price − Book value.**

**Without an asset disposal account** (depreciation credited to the asset): the sale is shown in the asset account itself. Charge depreciation to the date of sale, then credit the asset with the sale price, and with the loss (or debit it with the profit) to close the asset's book value; the result goes to the Profit and Loss A/c.

key_terms.definition_md: The excess of the sale price of an asset over its book value on the date of sale.
The shortfall of the sale price of an asset below its book value on the date of sale.

sections.heading: 8. The asset disposal account
sections.body_md:
When the asset is kept at cost with a provision account, a sale goes through an **Asset Disposal Account**. First provide depreciation on the asset sold up to the date of sale (Depreciation A/c Dr; To Provision for Depreciation A/c). Then:

1. Asset Disposal A/c Dr; To Asset A/c (**cost** of the asset sold).
2. Provision for Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset Disposal A/c (**accumulated depreciation** on that asset).
3. Bank A/c Dr; To Asset Disposal A/c (**sale price**).
4. The **balancing figure** is the profit (credit to Profit and Loss A/c) or loss (debit to Profit and Loss A/c).

The disposal account must **close with nothing left**. After a sale the provision holds only the depreciation of the assets still held; the asset account holds only their cost.

**Selling one of several assets:** only that asset's cost and accumulated depreciation leave the accounts; the others carry on.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually split (ISC Accounts)**
- 1 mark: the cause of depreciation in a case, a rate or a charge from a formula, the side of an entry, or the key of an assertion-reason item.
- 2 marks: a definition with a feature, two reasons or limitations, a depreciation figure with its working, or the two entries of a charge.
- 3 marks: a depreciation schedule for three years, journal entries for a year, a book value and profit or loss on sale, or an Asset Disposal A/c.
- 5 marks: asset and provision accounts for two or three years, with workings; or a sale through a disposal account. Step marks go for the working note, each year's account, the balancing and the result.

**Common mistakes**
- Counting a full year for a part-year purchase, or the wrong number of months.
- Applying the WDV rate to the cost after the first year.
- Forgetting to take the sold asset's depreciation out of the provision.
- Using the original cost instead of the book value to find the profit or loss.
- Forgetting depreciation up to the date of sale.
- Leaving out balance c/d and b/d in the ledger accounts.

cards.back_md: The fall in the book value of a fixed asset because it is used, charged as an expense of each year.
No. It is a non-cash charge; no money leaves the business when it is recorded.
To show the correct profit and the true value of the asset, to keep funds in the business and to match expense with income.
Wear and tear, passage of time, obsolescence and depletion.
Loss of value because a newer invention or design makes the asset out of date.
Loss of value of a wasting asset, such as a quarry, as the resource is taken out.
Not normally; land does not wear out.
Repairs keep the asset working; depreciation spreads its cost. They are different charges.

cards.front_md: Three factors that decide the amount of depreciation
cards.back_md: Cost, estimated useful life and residual (scrap) value.
Cost of the asset less the depreciation charged on it so far.
The same amount every year: (cost − scrap value) ÷ life in years.

cards.front_md: Rate of depreciation under the straight line method
cards.back_md: Annual depreciation ÷ cost × 100, on the original cost.
A fixed percentage of the opening book value of each year, so the charge falls.

cards.front_md: Does scrap value enter the WDV charge?
cards.back_md: No. The yearly charge is rate × opening book value.

cards.front_md: Does the WDV book value reach nil?
cards.back_md: No. It is multiplied by (1 − rate) each year, so a balance always remains.
Annual charge × months of use ÷ 12, counting the months exactly from the date of purchase or to the date of sale.

cards.front_md: Same rate, same cost: first-year charge
cards.back_md: The same under both methods; they differ from the second year.

cards.front_md: Which method suits furniture and buildings?
cards.back_md: The straight line method: even service over a fixed life.

cards.front_md: Which method suits vehicles and computers?
cards.back_md: The WDV method: they lose value fastest early and need more repairs later.

cards.front_md: Journal entry when depreciation is credited to the asset
cards.back_md: Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset A/c. The asset account shows the book value.

cards.front_md: Journal entry when a provision is kept
cards.back_md: Depreciation A/c Dr; To Provision for Depreciation A/c. The asset stays at cost.
Profit and Loss A/c Dr; To Depreciation A/c.
A credit-balance account that collects the depreciation on the assets held; it is deducted from the asset at cost in the balance sheet.

cards.front_md: Asset at cost and provision: what is the book value?
cards.back_md: Asset at cost less the balance of the Provision for Depreciation A/c.

cards.front_md: Depreciation on an asset added during the year
cards.back_md: Charge only for the months from the date of purchase to the year end.

cards.front_md: Book value at the date of sale
cards.back_md: Cost less the depreciation provided up to that date, including the part-year charge.
Sale price − book value: positive is a profit, negative is a loss.

cards.front_md: Where does a loss on sale go?
cards.back_md: It is debited to the Profit and Loss A/c; a profit is credited.
An account that collects the cost, the provision, the sale price and the profit or loss of an asset sold.

cards.front_md: Entries in the Asset Disposal A/c
cards.back_md: Cost debited; accumulated depreciation and sale price credited; the balancing figure is the profit or loss.

cards.front_md: After a sale, what does the provision hold?
cards.back_md: Only the depreciation of the assets still held; the sold asset's share has been transferred out.

questions.stem_md: A press of Karimnagar Cables, an imagined firm, is in perfect working order, but a faster press has come on the market and the firm expects to replace the old one within two years. The main cause of depreciation on the old press is

options.text_md: wear and tear
obsolescence
passage of time
depletion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** obsolescence. The press has not been worn out, so wear and tear is not the cause; it has no fixed term, so passage of time does not apply; and nothing is being extracted from it, so there is no depletion. Being overtaken by a better design is obsolescence.

questions.stem_md: Machinery of Erode Elastics, an imagined firm, cost ₹6,00,000. The Provision for Depreciation A/c shows a credit balance of ₹2,10,000 at the year end. In the balance sheet the machinery is shown as

options.text_md: machinery at ₹6,00,000 and a liability of ₹2,10,000 on the other side
machinery at ₹8,10,000, being cost plus provision
machinery at ₹2,10,000 only
machinery at ₹6,00,000 less provision ₹2,10,000, giving ₹3,90,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** machinery at ₹6,00,000 less provision ₹2,10,000, giving ₹3,90,000. The provision is a deduction from the asset, not a liability, so showing ₹6,00,000 with ₹2,10,000 as a liability is wrong. Adding the provision gives ₹8,10,000, which is above the cost. ₹2,10,000 alone ignores the cost.

questions.stem_md: Nagercoil Netting, an imagined firm, charges depreciation every year on its net-making machine. Depreciation is best described as

options.text_md: the gradual fall in the book value of a fixed asset because of its use, spread over its life
the fall in the market price of the asset on a given day
the money spent every year to repair the machine
a cash reserve kept aside to buy a new machine

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the gradual fall in the book value of a fixed asset because of its use, spread over its life. Depreciation is a charge for the use of the asset. A market-price fall, a repair bill and a cash reserve are separate ideas: a repair keeps the machine working, and no cash is set aside when depreciation is charged.

questions.stem_md: Gadag Gears, an imagined firm, bought a machine for ₹5,00,000 on 1 April 2026 and writes it down at 12% a year on the written down value. Depreciation for the year ended 31 March 2028 is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹52,800. Book value on 1 April 2027 = 5,00,000 − 60,000 = 4,40,000. Depreciation = 4,40,000 × 12% = ₹52,800. ₹60,000 is 12% of the cost (the first year), ₹1,12,800 adds the two years together, and ₹46,464 is the charge for the third year.

questions.stem_md: Salem Sacks, an imagined firm, charges depreciation through a Provision for Depreciation A/c. At the end of the third year the balance of that account equals

options.text_md: the depreciation charged in the third year alone
the book value of the assets held
the total depreciation charged up to that date on the assets still held
the cost of the assets held

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the total depreciation charged up to that date on the assets still held. The provision collects depreciation year after year, so it holds the accumulated amount, not one year's charge. Book value is cost less this balance, and cost is the balance of the asset account.

questions.stem_md: A lorry of Ongole Logistics, an imagined firm, cost ₹8,40,000 and the depreciation provided on it up to the date of sale was ₹3,36,000. It was sold for ₹4,90,000. The result on sale is

options.text_md: a loss of ₹14,000
a profit of ₹14,000
a profit of ₹1,54,000
a loss of ₹3,50,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a loss of ₹14,000. Book value = 8,40,000 − 3,36,000 = 5,04,000, which is above the price of 4,90,000. A profit of ₹1,54,000 compares the price with the depreciation instead of the book value, and a loss of ₹3,50,000 compares it with the original cost.

questions.stem_md: A stone quarry of Tumakuru Granites, an imagined firm, yields less stone every year as the stone is taken out. The fall in the value of the quarry is a case of

options.text_md: obsolescence
passage of time
wear and tear of a machine
depletion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** depletion. A wasting asset is used up as the resource is removed, which is depletion. The quarry does not become out of date, its value does not depend on the end of a term, and it is not a machine that wears.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following does NOT directly decide the yearly charge by the straight line method for a boiler bought by Bidar Boilers, an imagined firm?

options.text_md: The cost of buying and installing the boiler
The price the boiler would fetch in the market on the last day of the year
The number of years the firm expects to use it
The scrap value expected at the end of its life

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The price the boiler would fetch in the market on the last day of the year. The formula uses cost, scrap value and life. A day-to-day market price is not an input, because depreciation is an allocation of cost and not a revaluation.

questions.stem_md: A generator costing ₹4,00,000, with an expected scrap value of ₹40,000 and a life of 9 years, is bought by Thane Thermals, an imagined firm. The rate of depreciation by the straight line method on cost is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 10%. Annual charge = (4,00,000 − 40,000) ÷ 9 = 40,000, and 40,000 ÷ 4,00,000 × 100 = 10%. 11.11% comes from dividing 4,00,000 by 9 without deducting the scrap value; 90% forgets to divide by the life; 9% confuses the life with the rate.

questions.stem_md: Kovilpatti Kilns, an imagined firm, bought a kiln for ₹2,70,000 on 1 June 2027 and depreciates it at 10% a year on cost. Books close on 31 March. Depreciation for the year ended 31 March 2028 is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹22,500. June to March is 10 months: 2,70,000 × 10% × 10/12 = 22,500. ₹27,000 charges a full year, ₹24,750 counts 11 months, and ₹20,250 counts only 9 months.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following statements about the written down value method, as used by Palwal Pumps, an imagined firm, is correct?

options.text_md: The charge is the same every year
Scrap value is deducted from cost before the rate is applied
The yearly charge falls as the book value falls, because a fixed rate is applied to the opening book value
The book value reaches zero at the end of the asset's life

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The yearly charge falls as the book value falls, because a fixed rate is applied to the opening book value. The base shrinks every year, so the charge shrinks too. An equal yearly charge describes the straight line method, scrap value is not part of the written down value calculation, and the book value is multiplied by one minus the rate each year, so it never reaches zero by itself.

questions.stem_md: Dhubri Dyes, an imagined firm, credits depreciation straight to its Machinery A/c. After three years the balance of that account represents

options.text_md: the original cost of the machinery
the depreciation charged so far
the price the machinery will fetch on sale
the book value of the machinery

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the book value of the machinery. Each credit reduces the debit balance, so what remains is cost less depreciation to date. The cost is the figure only under the provision method, the depreciation charged is the provision balance, and the future sale price is an estimate not recorded here.

questions.stem_md: Rajkot Rollers, an imagined firm, keeps its machinery at cost with a Provision for Depreciation A/c and sells one machine during the year. Which treatment of the provision account is correct?

options.text_md: Credit it with the sale price of the machine
Leave it unchanged, since the Machinery A/c has been credited with the cost
Debit it with the loss on sale
Debit it with the accumulated depreciation on the machine sold, taking the amount to the Asset Disposal A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Debit it with the accumulated depreciation on the machine sold, taking the amount to the Asset Disposal A/c. The provision still holds depreciation of an asset that has gone, so that amount is removed and it forms one side of the disposal account. The sale price is credited to the disposal account and not to the provision, leaving it unchanged would overstate the provision, and the loss on sale belongs to the profit and loss account.

questions.stem_md: In the Asset Disposal A/c of Sikar Springs, an imagined firm, the machine sold is debited at its cost of ₹3,60,000, and the accumulated depreciation of ₹1,44,000 and the sale price of ₹1,90,000 are credited. The balancing figure is

options.text_md: a profit of ₹26,000, credited to the Profit and Loss A/c
a loss of ₹1,70,000
a loss of ₹26,000, debited to the Profit and Loss A/c
a profit of ₹46,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a loss of ₹26,000, debited to the Profit and Loss A/c. Debit side 3,60,000; credit side 1,44,000 + 1,90,000 = 3,34,000. The credit side is short by 26,000, which is the loss. A profit of the same size has the wrong direction; ₹1,70,000 compares the price with cost; ₹46,000 compares the price with the depreciation alone.

questions.stem_md: Lonavala Lamps, an imagined firm, bought a machine for ₹2,00,000 on 1 April 2026 and wrote it down at 10% a year on the written down value. It sold the machine on 31 March 2028 for ₹1,70,000. The result on sale is

options.text_md: a loss of ₹10,000
a profit of ₹8,000
a profit of ₹10,000
a loss of ₹8,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a profit of ₹8,000. Year 1: 20,000, so 1,80,000 is left; year 2: 10% of 1,80,000 = 18,000, leaving 1,62,000. Price 1,70,000 − 1,62,000 = ₹8,000. A loss of ₹10,000 forgets the second year, and a profit of ₹10,000 uses straight line book value of 1,60,000.

questions.stem_md: Which one of these fixed assets of Pathankot Printers, an imagined firm, would normally not be depreciated?

options.text_md: Freehold land on which the press shed stands
The delivery van
The printing machine
Office furniture

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Freehold land on which the press shed stands. Land does not wear out or become obsolete, so no depreciation is normally charged on it. A van, a machine and furniture all lose value with use.

questions.stem_md: Neemuch Nuts, an imagined firm, had machinery costing ₹3,00,000 on 1 April 2027 and bought more for ₹1,20,000 on 1 January 2028. It charges 10% a year on cost. Total depreciation for the year ended 31 March 2028 is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹33,000. Old machinery: 3,00,000 × 10% = 30,000. New machinery for 3 months: 1,20,000 × 10% × 3/12 = 3,000. Total 33,000. ₹42,000 gives the new machinery a full year, ₹30,000 leaves it out, and ₹39,000 counts 9 months instead of 3.

questions.stem_md: Sambhal Steels, an imagined firm, is choosing between the two methods for a furnace costing ₹4,00,000 at 20% a year. Over the first three years the straight line method charges how much more depreciation than the written down value method?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹44,800. Straight line: 3 × 80,000 = 2,40,000. Written down value: 80,000 + 64,000 + 51,200 = 1,95,200. The difference is 44,800. ₹1,95,200 and ₹2,40,000 are the two totals themselves, and ₹51,200 is only the third-year charge of the written down value method.

questions.stem_md: In the books of Cuddalore Clocks, an imagined firm, the Provision for Depreciation A/c is

options.text_md: an account with a credit balance, deducted from the asset at cost in the balance sheet
an asset account with a debit balance
an expense account closed to the profit and loss account at the year end
a cash fund kept in the bank to replace the asset

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** an account with a credit balance, deducted from the asset at cost in the balance sheet. It is a credit balance that reduces the asset. The depreciation expense account is a different account, and no cash or bank balance is set aside by this account.

questions.stem_md: Silchar Stoves, an imagined firm, sold a fixed asset for less than its book value on the date of sale. The resulting loss is

options.text_md: credited to the Profit and Loss A/c
added to the cost of the next asset bought
debited to the Profit and Loss A/c
carried forward as an asset in the balance sheet

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** debited to the Profit and Loss A/c. A loss is an expense of the year and reduces profit, so the Profit and Loss A/c is debited. A credit is for a profit, and a loss is never capitalised into another asset.

questions.stem_md:

**Assertion (A):** Wokha Warehouses, an imagined firm, must depreciate its freehold land every year because land wears out through use.

**Reason (R):** Depreciation is charged only in the year in which the asset is sold.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.

**Assertion (A):** A machine of Tinsukia Tea Estates, an imagined firm, that is written down at 25% a year on the written down value never reaches a zero book value.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md: Under the written down value method, Hosur Harvesters, an imagined firm, applies the rate of 20% to the original cost of a machine in every year of its life.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The rate is applied to the book value at the start of each year, so the yearly charge falls. Using the original cost every year is the straight line method.

questions.stem_md: A van of Panipat Parcels, an imagined firm, is sold for less than its book value on the date of sale. The difference is a loss and is debited to the Profit and Loss A/c.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Book value higher than the price means a loss, and a loss is an expense of the year.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Land has an unlimited life and does not wear out, so depreciation is normally not charged on it.

questions.stem_md: The profit on the sale of a machine by Rewa Rubber Works, an imagined firm, is the sale price less the original cost of the machine.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.stem_md: Ambala Axles, an imagined firm, charges depreciation on its plant every year. Define depreciation and state one feature of it.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between crediting depreciation to the asset account and crediting it to a provision for depreciation account, as practised by Hospet Hammers, an imagined firm.

questions.stem_md: Kolar Kerosene Depot, an imagined firm, wants to know why it must charge depreciation before working out its profit. State two reasons.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each valid reason: correct profit, true asset value, funds kept for replacement, or matching.

questions.stem_md: Gaya Gears, an imagined firm, is reviewing the depreciation on its fixed assets. (a) What is meant by obsolescence and by depletion? Give one example of each [2]. (b) State three factors that decide the amount of depreciation on a machine [3].
questions.solution_md: Marks for each meaning with its example, and for each factor with its effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Obsolescence: the asset loses value because a newer design or process has made it out of date, although it is not worn out. For example, a printing press replaced by a faster model.

Depletion: a wasting asset loses value as the resource in it is taken out. For example, a stone quarry from which stone is removed each year.

**(b)** 1. The cost of the machine, including carriage and installation: a higher cost gives a higher charge.

2. The estimated useful life: a longer life gives a lower yearly charge.

3. The estimated scrap value: a higher scrap value leaves less to be written off.
